Question: You are using a micro gas chromatograph with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and helium as the carrier gas to measure a gas sample with N2, O2, CO, and CH4. If you have a new sample that also contains a high concentration of H2, how can you measure the hydrogen content considering that the thermal conductivity of these gases follows the order H2 > He > CH4 > O2 > N2 > CO?

Options:
A. You can measure it, but you will obtain a negative peak for H2
B. You cannot detect hydrogen using helium as the carrier gas
C. You need to increase the measurement time of the chromatogram in order to detect H2
D. Your need to calibrate your gas chromatograph including H2 to establish a new zero baseline common to all gases

Thought: A thermal conductivity detector (TCD) works by measuring the difference in thermal conductivity between the carrier gas and the sample components. The detector response is proportional to the difference in thermal conductivity between the carrier gas and the analyte.

Looking at the thermal conductivity order given: H2 > He > CH4 > O2 > N2 > CO

When using helium as a carrier gas:
- Gases with lower thermal conductivity than helium (CH4, O2, N2, CO) will produce positive peaks
- Gases with higher thermal conductivity than helium (H2) will produce negative peaks

This is because when a component with lower thermal conductivity than helium passes through the detector, the filament temperature increases (less heat is carried away), resulting in a positive signal. Conversely, when hydrogen (which has higher thermal conductivity than helium) passes through, more heat is carried away from the filament, resulting in a negative peak.

Therefore, hydrogen can be detected using helium as a carrier gas, but it will produce a negative peak rather than a positive one.
Final Answer: [ANSWER]A[/ANSWER]
